extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and policymakers interested in the quality and evaluation of scientific peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying quality dimensions and empirical findings for evaluating scientific peer review systems (reliability, validity, fairness, efficiency, predictive power) to inform editorial policy and meta-research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability (Inter-rater reliability)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bornmann's meta-analysis of 48 studies reports 'a low level of inter-rater reliability.' However, low agreement is not necessarily undesirable because it may arise from different reviewers bringing different types of expertise and focusing on different aspects of a manuscript. Reliability can be measured using inter-rater statistics and should be interpreted in context of reviewer diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity (Predictive validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictive accuracy of editorial decisions informed by peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bornmann presents evidence (Angewandte Chemie International Edition study) that peer review is useful for manuscript selection: 78% of submissions accepted by AC-IE are correctly accepted for publication when the editor's decision is based on peer review. Validity here refers to how well peer-review-based decisions predict appropriate publication outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness (Absence of bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which the review process is free from systematic biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bornmann documents several types of bias observed in peer review processes: gender bias, geographic/institutional bias, cronyism in panel review, and selection bias against innovation. Evaluations should look for these biases and reviewers/editors should be aware of and attempt to mitigate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Speed and cost of the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficiency covers turnaround time and resource/costs associated with review. It is a quality dimension distinct from reliability and validity and should be measured and optimized when considering peer review workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive power (correlation with later citations/impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which peer-review assessments correlate with later scientific impact (e.g., citations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bornmann lists predictive power as a quality dimension, operationalized as correlation between review/selection decisions and downstream measures such as citation counts or other impact indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit criteria and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should provide explicit criteria for their judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bornmann recommends that reviewers give explicit criteria for their evaluations. Transparency about criteria helps interpret disagreements, improve consistency, and supports both the reliability and validity of decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of legitimate disagreement / diversity of expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledging that reviewer disagreement may reflect legitimate, complementary perspectives rather than error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bornmann emphasizes that different reviewers may focus on different manuscript aspects due to differing expertise; therefore, some level of disagreement can be appropriate. Editorial processes should recognize and value diverse expert perspectives rather than treating all disagreement as failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between reliability and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to achieve both agreement among reviewers and accurate, predictive editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bornmann argues reviewers and editors should strive for both reliability and validity. Policies should avoid optimizing one dimension (e.g., forcing consensus) at the expense of the other (e.g., reducing predictive accuracy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness for editorial decision-making (Decision accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which peer review aids editors in making correct accept/reject decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize as the proportion of editorial decisions that are 'correct' when judged against later outcomes or expert re-evaluation (the Angewandte example: 78% correctness when editors used peer review). This metric assesses the practical utility of peer review for selection.
